title: Replicants discover how robots learn and get tested — November 10, 2026: Children
lead: Cargo on wheels, movement examples and changed conditions reveal different difficulties.

news.title: A robot learns to push a cart without its hands upsetting its steps
news.summary: Researchers at China's Huazhong University of Science and Technology taught a humanoid to push a loaded cart. In a physical test it moved up to 30 kilograms of cargo supported by wheels, rather than lifted in its hands.
news.details: The hands need to help the same movement instead of pulling a shared handle in opposite directions. Software estimates the interaction from signals within the robot. A camera reads a special marker for the cart's direction. The robot therefore gets feedback about movement, rather than simply repeating one recorded gesture.
news.technical_novelty: Imagine a cart full of heavy things: you push its handle, and it pushes back against your hands. A robot must account for that effort too, or its steps may become unstable. Researchers first taught it to walk under different loads on its hands. They then added software that adjusts arms, waist and legs together.
news.engineering_impact: After computer training, the controller moved to a real machine without extra training on it. On a flat indoor floor, the robot pushed up to 30 kilograms of cargo at half a metre per second. Wheels support that weight; this was not a weightlifting test. Thresholds, slopes and unexpected obstacles would need separate checks.
news.limitations: After computer training, the controller moved to a real machine without extra training on it. On a flat indoor floor, the robot pushed up to 30 kilograms of cargo at half a metre per second. Wheels support that weight; this was not a weightlifting test. Thresholds, slopes and unexpected obstacles would need separate checks.
news.evidence_status: The researchers describe their own tests. Repetition by another team has not been confirmed.
news.organization: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
news.body:
Imagine a cart full of heavy things: you push its handle, and it pushes back against your hands. A robot must account for that effort too, or its steps may become unstable. Researchers first taught it to walk under different loads on its hands. They then added software that adjusts arms, waist and legs together.

The hands need to help the same movement instead of pulling a shared handle in opposite directions. Software estimates the interaction from signals within the robot. A camera reads a special marker for the cart's direction. The robot therefore gets feedback about movement, rather than simply repeating one recorded gesture.

After computer training, the controller moved to a real machine without extra training on it. On a flat indoor floor, the robot pushed up to 30 kilograms of cargo at half a metre per second. Wheels support that weight; this was not a weightlifting test. Thresholds, slopes and unexpected obstacles would need separate checks.

news.title: More examples helped a robot succeed more often
news.summary: NVIDIA presented a new robot-learning system at a scientific conference in Austin. Five demonstrations helped more than one in its tests, while computer-training speed was measured separately from machine movement.
news.details: Across fifty tested tasks, one demonstration of each job gave 71% average success. Five demonstrations gave 95%. This describes a particular test, not a promise that any home robot will complete 95 out of a hundred arbitrary chores. The model had already learned from large collections of human and robot recordings.
news.technical_novelty: To connect small parts carefully, a robot needs more than the ability to reach a table. It must choose an accurate movement. Demonstrations are examples of how work is done, and they can help teach it. The company introduced a model, a control program trained with data, together with tools for practice in a computer world.
news.engineering_impact: Another part of the announcement concerns simulation, a computer world for trying movements. New tools can account for cloth and cables changing shape. Training ran faster than an earlier configuration in one comparison. Computing attempts faster does not mean a real arm moves faster: its mechanism still has physical limits.
news.limitations: Another part of the announcement concerns simulation, a computer world for trying movements. New tools can account for cloth and cables changing shape. Training ran faster than an earlier configuration in one comparison. Computing attempts faster does not mean a real arm moves faster: its mechanism still has physical limits.
news.evidence_status: The company itself reports the tests, specifications or plans. The announcement supplies no independent verification.

Demonstrations are examples of how work is done, and they can help teach it. The company introduced a model, a control program trained with data, together with tools for practice in a computer world.

news.title: A robot test changes objects and places to check skills more fairly
news.summary: RLWRLD presented fifteen computer tests of robotic hand work in Seoul. Objects, their properties and their positions change, while comparison with physical robots is still planned.
news.details: The suite has fifteen tasks from retail, logistics, assembly and hotel food service. They include retrieving products, joining connectors, stacking plates and pouring liquid. A connector is a joining part, such as the end used to plug in a cable. Tests ask whether a skill still works with another object, different physical behaviour or a new location.
news.technical_novelty: Imagine a cup moved to the other side of a table. Repeating yesterday's hand movement will not be enough to pick it up. A robot can also work well in a familiar place and fail after a small change. The company prepared tests where such changes can be repeated and compared.
news.engineering_impact: For now, this happens in simulation, a computer world with rules for movement and contact. Objects use real-product specifications, but they are not therefore identical to reality. The company plans to compare results with physical robots. A real object might slip differently from its computer copy, changing how an action ends.

news.title: Gloves help record how a person controls two robot arms
news.summary: Tokyo's HumansX offered a two-arm robot setup with operator gloves. It is meant for control and recording examples, rather than announced as a robot that has already learned all the work by itself.
news.details: Each hand has twenty controlled movement directions, four per finger. This gives software more ways to position fingers than a simple gripper that only opens and closes. More possible movements do not mean the machine can choose them correctly by itself. An operator supplies the movement here, while the recordings prepare data for later work.
news.technical_novelty: A person wears special gloves and moves their fingers; robotic hands follow through a control system. Those actions can be recorded as demonstrations, examples for later learning. The company assembled two arms and offers setup. That can help users start recording without connecting every part of the equipment themselves.
news.engineering_impact: The next hand batch is expected from February 2027. Delivery of the complete setup depends on its configuration, with pricing available by enquiry. The announcement does not show a customer's task already learned autonomously from these recordings. A useful recording and an independently chosen action still require a separate learning and testing stage between them.

news.title: A Japanese company starts a four-legged robot for equipment checks
news.summary: Tokyo's RobotBank announced an industrial robot project for inspection rounds. It will first study working conditions; finished specifications and a sales date have not yet been announced.
news.details: Reaching the route's end is not enough: the inspection must return something useful. The company plans to measure task success, working time and how often a person helps. Safety and maintenance expense also matter. For now, those are planned measurements, not good scores already achieved by the new machine.
news.technical_novelty: A factory may need someone to follow the same route regularly and check equipment. A Japanese company plans to build a four-legged robot for that job. Legs may help on uneven ground, but the particular conditions matter. The developers therefore want to check each site's needs before choosing sensors and final specifications.
news.engineering_impact: Movement, body design and remote control will be developed together. Functions for recognising situations and doing tasks autonomously are intended as gradual additions after testing. A date for selling a finished machine is still unknown. This is a project's beginning; a picture of a similar robot cannot replace trials of this particular development.
